filename: Disentangling Hype from Reality for Artificial Intelligence–Based Skin Cancer Diagnosis-Comment on a Narrative Review.pdf
text: See related article on pg 492 Disentangling Hype from Reality for Artiﬁcial IntelligenceeBased Skin Cancer Diagnosis: Comment on a Narrative Review Crystal T. Chang1,2 and Roxana Daneshjou1,3 Journal of Investigative Dermatology (2024) 144, 444e445; doi:10.1016/j.jid.2023.07.026 T he explosion of claims around the performance of artiﬁcial intelligence (AI) for dermatology clouds the ability to separate the hype from the reality. In “Artiﬁcial intelligence in skin cancer diagnosis: a reality check,” Brancaccio et al (2023) review the state of image-based AI diagnostics in dermatology, with a particular focus on real- world impact for consumers, general practitioners, and dermatologists. Their review reveals that although there are plenty of opportunities and excitement around image- based AI for dermatology, there remains a signiﬁcant need for additional trials and evaluation in real-world settings. Despite the need for additional validation of image- based AI, numerous direct-to-consumer (DTC) applica- tions have already been released (Brancaccio et al, 2023). A survey conducted in the United Kingdom found that 41% of people would trust an AI-based application to diagnose skin cancers (British Association of Dermatologists, 2022). However, Brancaccio et al (2023) highlight prior work showing that the accuracy of these algorithms is variable on an independent test set of clinical images: of 25 apps available in 2022, mean diagnostic accuracy was between 50 and 60% (Brancaccio et al, 2023; Sun et al, 2022). Of note, newer consumer algo- rithms tested in early prospective trials in Austria showed some promise (sensitivity/speciﬁcity > 90%). However, such evidence is still preliminary and used physician- captured images rather than patient-captured images (Kra¨nke et al, 2023). Much of existing research on DTC AI applications is plagued by poor methodological quality, including high risk of bias, such as evaluation of high- quality images captured by clinicians as opposed to real- world patient images, and poor generalizability attribut- able to evaluation under artiﬁcial conditions, such as assessment of diagnostic accuracy in isolation without additional patient medical history (Brancaccio et al, 2023). Although transparency with regard to study design has improved after the publication of the SPIRIT (Standard Protocol Items: Recommendations for Interventional Trials) and CONSORT-AI (Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials-Artiﬁcial Intelligence) guidelines (Liu et al, 2020a; Rivera et al, 2020), AI developers are not required to list evidence supporting the diagnostic capabilities of their algorithms in the DTC interface, raising concerns about consumer deception, especially when important diagnostic information is delivered in the absence of adequate counseling by medical professionals (British Association of Dermatologists, 2022). Image-based AI diagnostics show some promise in aiding general practitioners and potentially improving access by enabling telemedicine. Brancaccio et al (2023) describe 2 previous studies in which nondermatologists reported beneﬁts/improvement in diagnostic accuracy with AI assistance. However, in general, algorithms perform poorly on images underrepresented in their training datasets, which tend to consist of common con- ditions on fair skin in idealized settings rather than the full clinical spectrum of disease on diverse skin tones (Daneshjou et al, 2022). Research for augmenting dermatologist performance is more plentiful but indicates that we are still in the early days of deciphering what tools will actually provide meaningful clinical impact. Studies evaluating AI against dermatologists have been conducted in artiﬁcial settings that are not reﬂective of real-world practice. In fact, when AI models are pitted against dermatologists in a real-world setting, the dermatologists outperform the models (Brancaccio et al, 2023). However, what is needed now is additional prospective trials where dermatologisteAI collaboration is tested in real-world clinical settings to ensure patient beneﬁt. As we look toward the future, although standalone image-based diagnostic algorithms have their advantages, the ﬁeld is increasingly moving toward algorithms that more closely parallel the working model of the clinician, who (i) synthesizes multiple sources of information and (ii) references trusted text resources to arrive at a ﬁnal diagnosis and treatment plan. The ﬁrst half of this anal- ogy can be done by multimodal models, which can, in theory, incorporate multiple inputs and input types, such as images, medical history, laboratory results, pathology interpretation, genomics, and time course, into the ﬁnal diagnosis. Early examples of multimodal models include work by Liu et al (2020b), whose model included images and clinical information such as patient demographics and clinical history. The second half of the analogy can be seen with large language models that use retrieval- augmented generation (RAG), which combines the generative power of large language models with non- generative retrieval models that serve as an open-book source of knowledge. Besides enabling a higher degree of accuracy by conditioning outputs on high-quality sources (rather than the entire Internet), RAGs (such as Clinfo.ai, which references PubMed in a manner roughly analogous to a clinician who consults PubMed or UpToDate) can also provide the end user with the pas- sages the model used to derive its answer, increasing transparency and simplifying the veriﬁcation process (Lozano et al, 20231). In summary, although the ﬁeld of image-based diagnostics is rapidly evolving, current research is insufﬁcient to suggest deﬁnite clinical utility. Perhaps the most evidence exists for dermatologist-focused augmented intelligence applications, although even within this indication, more robust studies will be needed to adequately assess real-world value and safety. Future studies should focus on increasing transparency and real-world validation (in terms of conditions seen, diverse skin tones, and realistic study workﬂows). With the rise of large language models and multimodal large-scale models, the future of AI in dermatology will also likely include models that incorporate multiple sources of information, more closely mimicking clinician workﬂows. Clinical Implications � Lack of transparency, biased training datasets, and evaluation under artiﬁcial conditions limit the strength of current evidence for image-based artiﬁcial intelligence (AI) diagnostics. � Direct-to-consumer applications have the least robust evidence, whereas dermatologists may not uniformly beneﬁt from AI assistance. � Other types of foundation models may be useful for improving explainability, training data, and accuracy.
